crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit
children.blurb: The AI enablement audit is a structured review of how an organization can safely adopt or expand AI systems.

children.name: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
children.blurb: Threat modelling for legal AI is the structured practice of identifying, ranking, and documenting plausible failure and attack paths in AI systems used for legal work, such as document review, legal research, contract analysis, and client communication.

children.name: Data Loss Prevention and Sanitisation
children.blurb: Data loss prevention and sanitisation in AI security audits covers the controls that stop sensitive or regulated information from entering model training sets, prompts, retrieval contexts, or generated outputs.

children.name: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
children.blurb: Shadow AI in legal teams covers any AI tool or model that lawyers, paralegals, or legal operations staff use without formal approval from the firm's IT, security, or compliance function.

children.name: Bias Testing and Alignment
children.blurb: Bias testing and alignment covers evaluating model outputs for unfair treatment across protected attributes and checking whether model behavior matches organizational or legal expectations.

sections.body: This field is the practical work of checking whether legal teams can use AI tools without breaking confidentiality, privilege, or fairness rules. It is not about hypothetical risks. Right now, artificial intelligence is being used inside law firms and corporate legal departments to draft, review, and summarize documents, and the audit work tests those specific systems before and after deployment. Enablement audits look at what a model is allowed to access, who can prompt it, and where its outputs go. Threat modelling for legal models maps how a prompt or a training data leak could expose client matter details. Data loss prevention and sanitisation tools scrub or block sensitive text before it leaves a firm's control. Shadow AI in legal teams means staff using unapproved chatbots or summarizers, and bias testing checks whether a model treats parties, jurisdictions, or protected classes unevenly.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is maturing but uneven. Some parts are solved well enough for routine use, such as basic data loss prevention filters that catch Social Security numbers or bank details, and simple access logging for approved tools. What is not solved is reliable detection of shadow AI, because staff can use personal devices or consumer chat interfaces that leave no audit trail. Bias testing for legal language is still early, with no agreed benchmark for what a fair legal summary looks like across different case types. The honest limit is that no audit can guarantee a model will not leak or misstate something under a novel prompt. The site's tracking of 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 6825 state AI bills shows that the legal exposure is real and changing faster than most internal policies.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with The AI Enablement Audit, which gives the overall checklist for deciding whether a legal AI tool is safe to turn on. From there, Threat Modelling for Legal AI goes deeper into specific failure paths, such as prompt injection or training data memorisation, and is the page for security staff who need to draw attack trees. Data Loss Prevention and Sanitisation is the practical companion for IT teams that must configure filters and redaction before any model sees client text. Shadow AI in Legal Teams addresses the human side, how to find and measure unapproved use that bypasses those technical controls. Bias Testing and Alignment closes the loop by examining whether a model that is technically secure still produces unfair or misaligned legal outputs, which matters for ethics and court credibility.
